DWM SPECIAL UPDATE ABOUT WEST PACIFIC TYPHOON DATED 8TH NOVEMBER, 2025

#Topic: Back-to-Back Strong Typhoons in the Western Pacific, Late flourish cyclone trend continues...

Do you know the fact?

1. September: Active Hurricane season of Atlantic Ocean.
2. October: Active Typhoon season of Pacific Ocean.
3. November: Active Cyclone season of North Indian Ocean.
============================

Historical closure of Atlantic basin

==> Much like the Northeast Monsoon's current behavior, the Atlantic hurricane season also experienced a very slow start this year. 

==> September was unusually inactive, but the season concluded on a historical note with Hurricane #Melissa, which brought one of the worst disasters to #Jamaica.
============================

Back to back typhoons at west pacific ocean

==> In a similar pattern, the Western Pacific typhoon season remained quiet through much of October. However, within just a week, the basin has unleashed two powerful back to back typhoons.

==> Typhoon #Kalmaegi recently caused severe devastation across the Philippines and Vietnam, claiming over 188 lives in the Philippines alone, with dozens more affected in Vietnam through flooding, landslides, and storm surges.

==> Now, Typhoon #FungWong has rapidly intensified into a massive Category 4 typhoon and is posing a serious threat to northern Philippines within the next 36 hours.

==> After making landfall in North Philippines, it is forecast to track northeastward toward the South China Sea and Taiwan coasts, with significant weakening expected along the way.
============================

Northeast Monsoon getting into Active phase!

==> Following this intense activity, the Western Pacific is likely to enter sleep mode, shifting focus to the Bay of Bengal. We anticipate a series of back to back rain bearing systems there, particularly between November 20th and November 30th, 2025.

==> Before that, good rainfall is probable over our region from an easterly wave with trough of low or a possible weak low during November 15th-20th. Dry line storms should be watchable at Coastal region on Nov 11th & 12th, 2025.
============================

Negative IOD base state will bring Magic!

==> The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) has currently weakened over the Pacific as it fighted with La-Nina it's became dead soon but it is expected to reinitiate over the eastern Indian Ocean after November 20th. 

==> With the negative Indian Ocean Dipole (NIOD) peak has already surpassed, planetary waves such as Kelvin and Equatorial Rossby waves will continue supporting this base state of Negative IOD.

==> Overall, events are unfolding exactly as anticipated earlier. After a very weak beginning, the Northeast Monsoon is set to Roar back strongly during the second half of November.

Late flourish Atlantic, Pacific and next North Indian ocean..

"It's never too late to be what you might have been"
============================

Thanks & Regards
Hemachander R

To everyone in the Philippines, those who may be affected by the typhoon or flooding, I know it has brought great hardship. Please stay mindful, take care of yourselves, and value your lives above all. 

Wish for everyone’s safety🥺🙏🏻

#Fungwong #UwanPH

Typhoon Fung-Wong, locally known as Uwan in the Philippines, is the 26th named storm of the 2025 Pacific typhoon season and a rapidly intensifying tropical cyclone currently barreling across the Philippine Sea. It formed earlier this week and was officially upgraded to typhoon status by weather agencies on Friday evening, just hours after the previous storm, Typhoon Kalmaegi, was downgraded.
Current Status and Intensity
As of Saturday morning (November 8, 2025), Fung-Wong has sustained winds of 140 km/h (87 mph) with gusts reaching up to 170 km/h (106 mph). Its massive circulation spans approximately 1,500 km (932 miles) in diameter—large enough to blanket nearly the entire Philippines with rain and wind. Forecasters from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center and the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) predict it could escalate to super typhoon strength (winds of at least 185 km/h or 115 mph) before landfall.
Path and Forecast
The typhoon is moving westward toward the eastern coast of the Philippines and is expected to make landfall on Sunday (November 9), potentially near Legazpi City in the Bicol Region. After crossing Luzon, it may continue into the South China Sea, affecting southern Vietnam later in the week. Its expansive size means impacts could extend across Luzon (including Manila), the Visayas islands, and even as far as Siargao in the east.
Expected Impacts and Warnings
Fung-Wong poses significant threats of violent winds, life-threatening storm surges (up to 3-5 meters in coastal areas), and heavy rainfall leading to widespread flooding and landslides. Low-lying and coastal communities are at highest risk, with PAGASA urging immediate evacuations to higher ground. Several airlines, including Philippine Airlines, have already canceled flights, and all marine activities have been suspended nationwide. The storm's arrival comes amid recovery efforts from recent disasters, exacerbating vulnerabilities in infrastructure and emergency response.
Broader Context
This is the second major typhoon to strike the Philippines in less than a week, following the deadly Typhoon Kalmaegi (local name: Kristine), which killed nearly 200 people in the central Philippines—primarily from drowning in Cebu province—and five more in Vietnam. Kalmaegi's impacts were worsened by clogged waterways and delays in early warnings, displacing tens of thousands. Fung-Wong marks the 21st named storm to affect the country this year, highlighting the Philippines' position in the typhoon belt and the increasing intensity of storms linked to climate change.
For real-time updates, track it via official sources like PAGASA or the Joint Typhoon Warning Center. If you're in the affected areas, prioritize safety and follow local evacuation orders.
